newsitem.title: UK: Trans-World sees Russian aluminium exports falling.
newsitem.headline: Trans-World sees Russian aluminium exports falling.

text.p: Exports of primary aluminium from Russia to the West are likely to drop to virtually nothing within the next decade, according to David Reuben, chairman of major aluminium player Trans-World Metals.
Internal consumption is set to grow while some less efficient producers could fall by the wayside, he said.
"Within ten years I would reckon Russia will not be an exporter of primary aluminium because it will not be able to feed its own population (with the metal)," Reuben told Reuters in an interview.
"What may happen is that uneconomical plants out of sync with modernity may eventually close down and plants which survive will get a better chance to produce and sell their own product," he said.

"With consumption going up, you will find the raw materials starting to be used inside of Russia," Reuben added. He forecast Russian consumption to rise 10 to 15 percent in the next two to three years.
Reuben said Russian aluminium demand was already showing signs of growth, particularly in the construction industry.
And exports outside the CIS tended to be overstated anyway.
At maximum capacity aluminium smelters in Russia could produce 2.4 million tonnes annually, of which 500,000 tonnes is sold internally, he explained.
"In my opinion exports will be between 1.8 and 1.9 million tonnes (in 1996)," he said.
He also disagreed with some analysts who said Russia was drawing on internal stocks in order to boost export levels.
"There has never been a stockpile anywhere during the last five years that I know of in Russia," he said.
Reuben said he was comfortable about Trans-World's deep involvement in Russian industry.
"Yes we are comfortable investing in Russia because we have built infrastructure and facilities over the years that makes it easier having gone through the early risks."
He said all business involved risk, and ignoring the Russian aluminium industry was a risk in itself.
"If people ignore it, they exclude it from their thinking about what value to put on their own production. Even if you don't want to invest in Russia, you should not ignore it."
Reuben said Trans-World's investment in Russia was broadly a success, although weak world aluminium prices were putting pressure on profit margins.
"If the markets get much lower then we may start to see negative returns, but we will have to continue working," he said. "You have to take the rough with the smooth."
Reuben expected aluminium to recover soon, because Trans-World's order books picked up significantly from slow demand late in 1995 and early in 1996, particularly in Europe.
"We are finding demand a great deal higher today. Demand and premiums are hardening, and I am facing shortages in delivering. All of a sudden the right material is not in the right place."
Trans-World is a major commodities group with interests in aluminium, steel, ferro-alloys, fertilisers and energy products. It is also involved in infrastructure and construction projects.
Reuben said aluminium accounts for between 25 and 30 percent of the group's turnover, with annual worldwide sales anywhere between one and two million tonnes.
"From our own production, either where we are tolling or through different ownerships globally, we produce aluminium somewhere to the tune of 800,000 to 1.2 million tonnes."
Trans-World is looking at new projects all over the globe.
"We are looking at further investments," he said.

Reuben said the company was looking at a third expansion phase at the Pavlodar alumina complex in Kazakhstan. A new plant would be built to boost output to two million tonnes from the current rate of 1.35 million tonnes.
The alumina would be used to feed planned expansions at the giant Russian aluminium smelters of Bratsk and Sayansk.
